newsitem.title: POLAND: POLAND'S MASS PRIVATISATION FUNDS HIT BOURSE.
newsitem.headline: POLAND'S MASS PRIVATISATION FUNDS HIT BOURSE.

text.p: Poland's 15 National Investment Funds (NFIs) started bourse trade on Thursday adding muscle to the Polish market and giving it the last say in an ongoing debate on the country's landmark mass privatisation scheme.

Government, bourse and fund officials hailed the opening session as a success for Poland's trademark programme in which the funds were given a role of surrogate strategic investors for more than 500 companies privatised in one go.
The bourse president Wieslaw Rozlucki told a news conference after the market close that the fund's addition would make the stock market more attractive by boosting its capitalisation.
"The market's capitalisation grows by five billion zlotys to 35 billion...this bodes well for the equity market and for the upcoming biggest privatisations," Rozlucki said.
Deputy treasury minister Ewa Freyberg, also present, said the funds now faced the ultimate challenge of living up to market expectations.

"Now the funds become self-reliant and the influence of the ministry will be smaller while the challenges for NFIs will be of economic and not political nature," said Freyberg, who oversaw the implementation of the programme.

Analysts said the addition of the funds might shift investor attention from stocks for some time but in the longer-run should help the market as a whole by attracting new players to the Warsaw market.

They said that for big institutional investors the very increase in capitalisation was a positive signal while an introduction of an entirely new instrument could bring in a new class of players investing in closed-ended funds.
"Those NFIs are managed by experienced management companies...and I think that would be seen as a positive," said Geoffrey Skipper, chief strategist at Korona mutual fund company.
Analysts also said that the funds heavy on industrial stocks offered an attractive opportunity to gain exposure to Poland's fast growing manufacturing sector.
But some said foreigners might stay on the sidelines, waiting for more liquid trade to enter the fray.

"I think initially those foreign investors who hold the vouchers...unless they are particularly aggressive, they will be watching and waiting for the dust to settle," said Stephen Pettyfer, an analyst at Merrill Lynch in London.

The all-share NFI price index calculated as a sum of share prices of all 15 funds opened at 160 at a premium to NFI units exchangeable for 15 fund shares, one in each fund with prices of individual funds ranging from 13 to 7.85 zlotys.
Analysts said the spread between the prices of funds' shares and NFI units would trigger arbitrage eventually making valuations of both instruments converge.
But they said that even though trading volume at 34.6 million zloty proved much stronger than widely expected the fund prices would remain highly volatile.

"One will have to wait several sessions for prices to stabilise, for the time being there will be big price swings creating excellent opportunities for speculators," Dariusz Szepieniec of Bank Slaski brokerage said.
Some analysts said the market would have to wait at least until half-year reports to evaluate the funds more precisely.
"For now it's all guessing which fund is worth," said Pawel Tarnowski of Raiffeisen Capital and Investment Polska.
